result.summary: Pindar celebrates Telesikrates of Kyrene, winner of the race in armour at Pytho in 478. He tells how Apollo carried off the huntress Kyrene to Libya, then briefly praises Thebes and Herakles, and ends with the tale of Alexidamos, who won a Libyan bride in a foot-race.

scenes.title: Editor's introduction
scenes.summary: The editor explains the race in armour, the date of the victory and the probable setting of the ode.

scenes.title: Proclaiming the victory
scenes.summary: Pindar says he wishes to proclaim Telesikrates' victory at Pytho, which has crowned Kyrene.

scenes.title: Apollo carries off Kyrene
scenes.summary: Apollo takes the huntress Kyrene from Pelion to Libya, where Aphrodite joins them. Her father is Hypseus of the Lapithai, and she fights wild beasts.
scenes.stakes: Kyrene is taken from her home and independence.

scenes.title: Apollo and Cheiron talk
scenes.summary: Apollo sees Kyrene fighting a lion and asks Cheiron about her. Cheiron foretells her future in Libya and the birth of Aristaios, and the marriage is made that day.

scenes.title: Return to Telesikrates
scenes.summary: Pindar links the victory to Kyrene's city and notes the value of brevity.

scenes.title: Thebes, Herakles and Iolaos
scenes.summary: Pindar recalls Iolaos burying Eurystheus at Thebes and praises Herakles. He says he has praised Kyrene before and urges praise of good deeds.

scenes.title: Telesikrates' earlier wins
scenes.summary: Maidens have watched Telesikrates win at many games and wished for such a husband or son.

scenes.title: Alexidamos wins the bride
scenes.summary: Antaios sets his daughter as prize in a foot-race, as Danaos once did. Alexidamos wins her and leads her away.
scenes.stakes: Suitors compete for the bride and the glory of winning her.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable line on the swiftness of gods' deeds.
Vivid image of Apollo's total knowledge.

analysis.text: The ode links an athletic victory to a founding myth: Kyrene's marriage to Apollo parallels Telesikrates' likely marriage and glorifies his city.
Victory odes were commissioned to praise winners and their cities; the race in armour trained for hoplite warfare.

legacy.text: The story of Apollo and Kyrene became the foundation legend of Cyrene in Libya, and her son Aristaios appears in Virgil's Georgics.

fun_facts.text: The race in armour (hoplitodromos) was introduced at Delphi's Pythian Games in 498 BC, according to the editor's note.

language_notes.text: Marathon (490 BC) was where Athenian hoplites charged the Persians at a run; Pindar's audience would know this famous victory.
Pytho is the older name for Delphi, where the Pythian Games were held in Apollo's honour.
'The third part of the mainland' means Libya, counted as the third continent beside Europe and Asia.
'Delian stranger' is Apollo, born on Delos, here arriving as a newcomer in Libya.
'Son of Philyra' is Cheiron, the wise Centaur, whose mother was the nymph Philyra.
'Lovecraft' here means the cunning art of love; the wise 'keys' are the secret means of opening love's mysteries.
Agreus ('hunter') and Nomios ('shepherd') are cult titles of Aristaios, god of hunting and herding.
Pytho is the older name of Delphi, where the Pythian Games were held; Telesikrates won there, so Kyrene's name was proclaimed by the herald.
Iolaos was Herakles' nephew and companion. He killed Eurystheus, the king who had persecuted Herakles, and buried him at Thebes.
Spartoi means 'sown men', the warriors who sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Kadmos at Thebes. Amphitryon is called their guest because he was an exile there.
Dirke was a spring at Thebes; Herakles and his twin Iphikles were raised there.
The 'old god of the sea' is probably Nereus, whose wise saying is given next: praise even an enemy's good deeds if just.
'Feast of Pallas' is the Athenian festival of Athena. 'Ample-bosomed Earth' probably refers to games in honour of Earth, the goddess Gaia.
'Fain' means eager or glad; 'cull' means pick, as one picks fruit.
Danaos had fifty daughters; this ode says forty-eight were married by a foot-race, a wedding contest arranged at Argos.

context_notes.text: The race in armour (hoplitodromos) was run by men carrying shield and often helmet and greaves.
The Lapithai were a Thessalian people; Peneus is a Thessalian river-god, and Hypseus is his grandson through Kreüsa.
Cheiron, the Centaur, lived in a cave on Mount Pelion and was famed as a wise teacher of heroes.
Aristaios was a divine helper of farmers, beekeepers and herdsmen; Kyrene was his mother by Apollo.
Alkmene bore Herakles to Zeus and Iphikles to her husband Amphitryon on the same night, hence 'twin sons'.
Irasa was a place in Libya, near Kyrene. Antaios was its ruler, and his daughter's marriage is the myth told here.
Alexidamos is the winning suitor, and his victory parallels Telesikrates'. The Nomads are the nomadic Libyan tribes.

literary_notes.text: Kyrene is defined by contrast: she rejects loom and feasting for javelins and beasts, showing her fierce, unwomanly-for-her-time independence.
Cheiron gently teases Apollo, a god who cannot lie, for pretending to ask what he already knows.
Counting leaves and grains of sand expresses Apollo's boundless knowledge through exaggerated, vivid images.
A general maxim about the gods' swiftness explains how the marriage is arranged so quickly.
Victory is a 'fair flower of good luck' to which the city is wedded, joining marriage imagery to civic honour.
Pindar speaks of his own craft, justifying a shortened treatment as a mark of poetic tact.
The maidens' silent wishes show Telesikrates as admired and desirable, and flatter him through others' eyes.
The maiden as prize and goal of the race blends athletic victory with marriage, echoing Telesikrates' own triumph.
The showers of leaves and wreaths exaggerate the celebration to convey the hero's glory.
